name: South Africa
summary: Banks are prudentially regulated by the Prudential Authority (PA) in the South African Reserve Bank and conduct-regulated by the FSCA under the twin-peaks Financial Sector Regulation Act. The Financial Intelligence Centre administers the FIC Act, which expressly requires ongoing AML/CFT/CPF training (s 43) and a board-approved Risk Management and Compliance Programme (s 42). The PA and FSCA jointly issue standards such as Joint Standard 2 of 2024, which requires annual cyber awareness training and board training. The Information Regulator enforces POPIA, SARS receives FATCA/CRS reports, and FAIS imposes training and CPD on staff who advise on financial products.

regulators.name: Prudential Authority (South African Reserve Bank)
regulators.role: Prudential regulator of banks under the Banks Act and FSR Act; issues directives, guidance notes and (with the FSCA) joint standards, and supervises banks' AML/CFT compliance under the FIC Act.

regulators.name: Financial Sector Conduct Authority
regulators.role: Market conduct regulator for financial institutions including banks; issues conduct standards (including the Conduct Standard for Banks), administers FAIS fit and proper requirements and co-issues joint standards.

regulators.name: Financial Intelligence Centre
regulators.role: Financial intelligence unit and AML/CFT/CPF authority under the FIC Act; receives reports, publishes sanctions lists, and issues guidance notes and directives.

regulators.name: Information Regulator
regulators.role: Regulator under the Protection of Personal Information Act and the Promotion of Access to Information Act; receives breach notifications and registers information officers.

regulators.name: South African Revenue Service
regulators.role: Receives FATCA and CRS reports from reporting financial institutions under the Tax Administration Act.

regulators.name: National Credit Regulator
regulators.role: Regulator of credit providers under the National Credit Act, including responsible lending and reckless credit rules.

regulators.name: Department of Employment and Labour
regulators.role: Administers the Employment Equity Act (including the harassment code) and the Occupational Health and Safety Act.

programs.title: South Africa | FIC Act AML/CFT/CPF Compliance Awareness
programs.why: Banks are accountable institutions under the Financial Intelligence Centre Act. Section 43 requires ongoing training so employees can comply with the Act and the bank's Risk Management and Compliance Programme (RMCP), and failure to train is sanctionable under s 62. Section 42 requires a documented RMCP, made available to staff who handle transactions, which since 2022 must also cover proliferation financing.

references.provision: Section 43 (training) and section 62 (failure to provide training), as substituted by ss 29 and 48
references.note: Substituted s 43: an accountable institution must give its employees ongoing training so they can comply with the Act and with the parts of the Risk Management and Compliance Programme that apply to them; s 62 (as substituted) makes failure to train a non-compliance subject to administrative sanction.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)

references.note: Banks must develop, document, maintain and implement an RMCP covering ML/TF risk identification, assessment, monitoring and mitigation; the board or senior management must approve it, it must be reviewed regularly, and its documentation must be available to every employee involved in covered transactions.

references.title: General Laws (Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorism Financing) Amendment Act 22 of 2022 (Government Gazette 47815)
references.note: Extends the RMCP to proliferation financing risk, PEP determination, enhanced and simplified due diligence and group-wide programmes.

programs.title: South Africa | Terrorist Financing under POCDATARA and the FIC Act

programs.why: Terrorist financing is a crime under POCDATARA, widened in 2022, and banks must address TF risk in their RMCP under FIC Act s 42. The s 43 duty to train employees on the Act and the RMCP therefore covers recognising TF risk, reporting suspicions and applying sanctions screening.

audience: Senior managers who approve PEP relationships
programs.why: Sections 21F-21H require banks to identify foreign and domestic politically exposed persons and prominent influential persons, their family members and close associates, and to apply senior management approval and enhanced measures. audience: Sanctions screening and payments operations staff
programs.why: Beyond the UN regime enforced through the FIC Act, banks with international business manage exposure to other sanctions programmes (such as US and EU lists) through policy and screening rather than any South African training rule. The FIC Act duties to scrutinise clients against UN designations and to train staff on the Act support a sanctions screening competence.

programs.title: South Africa | Suspicious and Unusual Transaction Reporting (s 29)
programs.why: Section 29 places the duty to report suspicious and unusual transactions on anyone who carries on, manages or is employed by a business, not only on the institution, and prohibits tipping off. The RMCP must set out how reports are identified and made, and s 43 requires training so employees can meet these duties.

programs.title: South Africa | Recognising Unusual Transactions
programs.why: Because s 29 reporting duties fall on individual employees, staff must be able to recognise transactions with no apparent business or lawful purpose and unusual patterns. The RMCP must cover how such transactions are examined (s 42(2)(h)) and staff must be trained under s 43.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.note: The RMCP must provide for examining complex or unusually large transactions and unusual patterns without apparent business or lawful purpose, and for keeping written findings.

programs.title: South Africa | Transaction Monitoring and Alert Investigation
programs.why: The RMCP must cover ongoing account monitoring and the examination of unusual transactions with written findings (ss 21C and 42(2)(g)-(h)). Analysts who run these processes must be trained on them under s 43.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.note: Ongoing monitoring of business relationships, examination of complex, unusually large or unusual transactions and keeping written findings must be covered by the RMCP.

programs.title: South Africa | Risk-Based Approach and the Risk Management and Compliance Programme
programs.why: The FIC Act is built on a risk-based approach: the RMCP must enable the bank to identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and manage ML, TF and PF risk, state which elements do not apply and why, be board-approved and reviewed regularly. Training on the RMCP is required by s 43.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.note: The RMCP is the bank's risk-based framework; it must be approved at the highest level of authority, reviewed regularly and made available to employees involved in covered transactions.

programs.title: South Africa | FIC Act Record Keeping and Reporting (ss 22-28)
programs.why: Banks must keep client and transaction records for at least five years (ss 22, 22A and 23) and report cash transactions above the prescribed threshold (s 28) as well as terrorist and sanctioned property (s 28A). The RMCP must say how records are kept and reports made, and staff must be trained under s 43.

programs.why: Frontline staff carry out identification, verification and cash reporting and bear a personal s 29 reporting duty. Section 43 requires ongoing training so they can comply with the provisions and RMCP procedures that apply to their role, and the RMCP documentation must be made available to them (s 42(3)).

programs.title: South Africa | AML Governance for Boards, Senior Management and Compliance Officers (s 42A)
programs.why: Section 42A makes the board responsible for ensuring the bank and its staff comply with the FIC Act and the RMCP, requires a compliance function, and requires a person of sufficient competence and seniority to run it; failures are sanctionable under s 61B. The board must also approve the RMCP. No separate course is prescribed, but these duties require informed oversight.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.note: The board must ensure compliance with the Act and RMCP, a compliance function must assist it, and a sufficiently competent and senior person must be assigned to ensure the function is effective.

programs.title: South Africa | Anti-Corruption and Failure to Prevent (PRECCA s 34A)
programs.why: Since April 2024 a private-sector company commits an offence if anyone performing services for it pays or offers a bribe to win or keep business, unless it had adequate procedures to prevent this. The Act does not define those procedures or prescribe training, but training is a usual part of showing adequate procedures.

references.title: Judicial Matters Amendment Act 15 of 2023
references.issuer: Parliament (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
references.provision: Section 23, inserting section 34A into the Prevention and Combating of Corrupt Activities Act 12 of 2004
references.note: A private-sector company commits an offence if a person performing services for it gives or offers a prohibited gratification to win or keep business or an advantage, unless it had adequate procedures designed to prevent this.

programs.title: South Africa | Corporate Governance under the Banks Act (s 60B)
programs.why: The Banks Act requires the board and executive officers to maintain an effective corporate governance process suited to the bank's risks, and places fiduciary duties and a duty of care and skill on directors. These are competence requirements rather than a training rule.

references.title: Annexure A to Directive 1 of 2026: Banks Act, 1990 and Regulations (extracts)
references.note: Summarises the statutory duties: directors and executive officers owe a fiduciary duty and a duty of care and skill (s 60); the board must keep an effective corporate governance process (s 60B); the directors' affairs committee must regularly review the board's skills mix (s 64B).

references.title: Directive 1 of 2026 (D1/2026): Governance tenure
references.note: Replaces Directive 4 of 2018. The board-approved governance policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors, ongoing assessment of individual directors, and robust criteria so that only fit and proper people with the needed knowledge and skills are appointed.

programs.title: South Africa | Board Directors' Training and Governance (PA Directive 1 of 2026)
programs.why: Directive 1 of 2026, issued under Banks Act s 6(6), requires each bank and controlling company to implement a board-approved governance policy that ensures appropriate and ongoing training for directors and ongoing assessment of their effectiveness. This is an express training duty limited to directors.

references.title: Directive 1 of 2026 (D1/2026): Governance tenure
references.note: Replaces Directive 4 of 2018. The board-approved governance policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors, ongoing assessment of individual directors, and robust criteria so that only fit and proper people with the needed knowledge and skills are appointed.

references.title: Annexure A to Directive 1 of 2026: Banks Act, 1990 and Regulations (extracts)
references.note: Summarises the statutory duties: directors and executive officers owe a fiduciary duty and a duty of care and skill (s 60); the board must keep an effective corporate governance process (s 60B); the directors' affairs committee must regularly review the board's skills mix (s 64B).

programs.title: South Africa | Fit and Proper Directors and Executive Officers (Banks Act)
programs.why: Banks must appoint only fit and proper directors and executive officers, assess them before appointment and regularly afterwards, and notify the PA using form BA 020. Skills and experience are part of the test, but no specific training is prescribed beyond the ongoing directors' training in Directive 1 of 2026.

references.title: Directive 7 of 2022 (D7/2022): matters related to fit and proper assessment of directors and executive officers
references.note: Banks remain responsible for appointing fit and proper directors and senior managers, must assess them before appointment and regularly afterwards, and the criteria include relevant skills and experience; criminal background checks support the BA 020 submission.

references.title: Directive 1 of 2026 (D1/2026): Governance tenure
references.note: Replaces Directive 4 of 2018. The board-approved governance policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors, ongoing assessment of individual directors, and robust criteria so that only fit and proper people with the needed knowledge and skills are appointed.

programs.title: South Africa | Whistleblowing under the Protected Disclosures Act
programs.why: Since the 2017 amendments, every employer must authorise internal procedures for receiving and dealing with reports of impropriety and take reasonable steps to bring them to the attention of every employee and worker. This is an express awareness duty, though no frequency is set.

references.title: Protected Disclosures Act 26 of 2000 (as amended by Act 5 of 2017)
references.issuer: Parliament (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
references.note: Every employer must authorise internal procedures for receiving and dealing with reports of impropriety and take reasonable steps to make every employee and worker aware of them.

programs.title: South Africa | FAIS Fit and Proper Competence, Product Training and CPD
audience: Bank staff appointed as FAIS representatives
Financial advisers and product sales staff
programs.why: Where a bank's staff give advice or intermediary services on financial products (for example deposits or investments), they are FAIS representatives. The fit and proper determination requires class of business and product specific training before they start, regulatory examinations where applicable, and continuing professional development, with a competence register kept by the bank.

references.title: Determination of Fit and Proper Requirements for Financial Services Providers, 2017 (Board Notice 194 of 2017)
references.issuer: FSCA (formerly Registrar of Financial Services Providers)
references.note: FSPs, key individuals and representatives must be competent; the FSP must ensure they are appropriately trained on the FAIS Act and their products, complete class of business and product specific training before giving advice or intermediary services, and undertake continuous professional development.

programs.title: South Africa | Treating Customers Fairly under the Conduct Standard for Banks
programs.why: Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 for Banks, made by the FSCA under the Financial Sector Regulation Act, requires banks to embed fair treatment of customers in their governance and operations. The standard's own text could not be opened; the FSCA's 2025 review confirms how it is supervised. Staff awareness supports compliance but no separate training rule was verified.

references.title: Banking Sector Complaints Management Review Report (February 2025)
references.provision: Review of section 8 of Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 (Banks)
references.note: FSCA desktop review of how banks apply the complaints management principles in section 8 of the Conduct Standard for Banks; it records weak compliance on keeping complainants informed and says the FSCA will monitor proper employee training and standardised procedures.

programs.title: South Africa | Responsible Lending and Reckless Credit (National Credit Act)
programs.why: The National Credit Act requires credit providers to assess affordability and the consumer's understanding of the credit before lending and prohibits reckless credit. Staff who make these assessments need to know the rules, but the Act does not prescribe training.

references.title: National Credit Act 34 of 2005
references.note: Before granting credit, the credit provider must take reasonable steps to assess the consumer's understanding of the risks and costs, repayment history and financial means and obligations, and must not enter into a reckless credit agreement.

programs.title: South Africa | Complaints Management under the Conduct Standard for Banks (section 8)
programs.why: Section 8 of the Conduct Standard for Banks sets complaints management requirements, including recording, categorising, acknowledging and informing complainants and referring them to the ombud. The FSCA's 2025 review found weaknesses and said it would monitor proper employee training. The standard's text could not be opened to confirm an express training duty.

references.title: Banking Sector Complaints Management Review Report (February 2025)
references.provision: Review of section 8 of Conduct Standard 3 of 2020 (Banks)
references.note: FSCA desktop review of how banks apply the complaints management principles in section 8 of the Conduct Standard for Banks; it records weak compliance on keeping complainants informed and says the FSCA will monitor proper employee training and standardised procedures.

programs.title: South Africa | Sales Practices and Product Suitability (FAIS)
audience: Bank staff appointed as FAIS representatives
programs.why: Under the FAIS fit and proper determination, the bank must ensure representatives are trained on the Act and the products they sell, can judge whether a product suits a client's needs and capacity, and are supervised until competent. Staff who do not meet the competence requirements must not render financial services.

references.title: Determination of Fit and Proper Requirements for Financial Services Providers, 2017 (Board Notice 194 of 2017)
references.issuer: FSCA (formerly Registrar of Financial Services Providers)
references.note: FSPs, key individuals and representatives must be competent; the FSP must ensure they are appropriately trained on the FAIS Act and their products, complete class of business and product specific training before giving advice or intermediary services, and undertake continuous professional development.

programs.title: South Africa | Cybersecurity Awareness Training (Joint Standard 2 of 2024)
audience: All bank employees and system users
programs.why: Joint Standard 2 of 2024, in force for banks since 1 June 2025, requires a comprehensive cybersecurity awareness training programme for all users, refresher training at least annually, regular training on new content as risks evolve, and periodic review of the programme.

references.title: Joint Standard 2 of 2024: Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Requirements for Financial Institutions (published with Joint Communication 2 of 2024)
references.note: Applies to banks, mutual banks and controlling companies. programs.why: When there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information was accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person, the bank must notify the Information Regulator and affected data subjects as soon as reasonably possible. programs.why: Directive 4 of 2023 requires banks to implement the BCBS operational resilience principles as part of enterprise risk management under Regulation 39 of the Banks Act Regulations, with compliance due by 31 December 2024. programs.why: The 2022 Code of Good Practice under the Employment Equity Act covers all forms of workplace harassment. Employers should have harassment policies and procedures and should include harassment in orientation, education and training programmes. The Code uses advisory language, so this is a competence expectation rather than an express statutory duty.

programs.title: South Africa | Sexual Harassment Prevention (EEA Code of Good Practice)
programs.why: The 2022 Code replaced the 2005 sexual harassment code. It expects employers to adopt sexual harassment policies and procedures and to cover sexual harassment in orientation, education and training. It must be considered in interpreting the Employment Equity Act but does not itself impose a binding training duty.

notes: The General Laws (AML and Combating Terrorism Financing) Amendment Act 22 of 2022 and the POCDATARA Amendment Act 23 of 2022 were published on 29 December 2022 (commencement was phased; check individual sections): they added proliferation financing to the FIC Act RMCP, renamed PEP categories, tightened beneficial ownership rules and moved UN terrorism designations onto the FIC Act s 26A mechanism.

South Africa exited the FATF grey list on 24 October 2025 (National Treasury statement); the next FATF mutual evaluation is expected between 2026 and October 2027, so supervisors are likely to keep testing effectiveness, including training.

Joint Standard 1 of 2023 (IT governance and risk management) took effect on 15 November 2024 and Joint Standard 2 of 2024 (cybersecurity and cyber resilience) on 1 June 2025. Joint Notice 2 of 2026 prescribes the material IT and cyber incident template from 1 September 2026.

PA Directive 1 of 2026 (governance tenure, 25 February 2026) replaced Directive 4 of 2018 and requires a board policy covering ongoing directors' training; the PA and FSCA are also developing a joint governance standard.
PA Directive 4 of 2023 on operational resilience replaced Directive 10 of 2021 and set 31 December 2024 as the compliance date.
PRECCA s 34A (failure to prevent corrupt activities, with an adequate procedures defence) was inserted by the Judicial Matters Amendment Act 15 of 2023, in force since 3 April 2024.

The POPIA Regulations were amended with immediate effect on 17 April 2025 (GN 6126); the amended text is hosted on the Information Regulator's site, which blocks automated access, so whether the information officer's awareness-session duty was retained is unconfirmed.
The FIC replaced Guidance Note 7 with Guidance Note 7A (2025) and consulted on a Guidance Note 7B in 2026; the FIC website could not be reached, so these were not verified or cited.
SARS reports revised CRS regulations (Notice R.6886, 28 November 2025) effective 1 March 2026; not verified because sars.gov.za blocked automated access.
